claim: In 1848 a railroad foreman named Phineas Gage had a 3-foot iron rod blown clean through his skull. He survived for 12 more years. His personality changed forever, and the case founded modern neuroscience.

In 1937 a defrocked English priest named Harold Davidson was mauled to death by a lion in a sideshow at Skegness. He had spent five years protesting his innocence after a scandal stripped him of his church, exhibiting himself in a barrel on Blackpool seafront and finally re-enacting Daniel in the Lions' Den live in a cage with two lions. The lions did not play along.

In 1962 a Soviet submarine officer named Vasili Arkhipov refused to authorise a nuclear torpedo launch during the Cuban Missile Crisis. He was outvoted 2 to 1, and his veto is the only reason World War 3 did not begin that day.

Sarah Winchester, heir to the Winchester rifle fortune, believed she was haunted by the dead. She built a 161-room mansion with stairs to nowhere and doors opening onto walls, with construction running 24 hours a day for 38 years.
In 2003 a hiker pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon used a dull multitool to amputate his own arm. Aron Ralston then rappelled down a cliff and walked 8 miles before being airlifted to safety.

Early 20th-century factory girls painted glow-in-the-dark watch dials with radium paint. Told to lick their brushes for a sharp tip, many died slowly of radiation poisoning. Their lawsuit established workers' rights to know what materials they handle.
Until 1986, women in Switzerland needed their husband's written permission to take a paid job. Married women were legally subordinate to their husbands until a sweeping reform that year.
In 1945 and 1946 the same plutonium sphere killed two Manhattan Project scientists in separate criticality accidents. They named it the Demon Core.
The mantis shrimp punches with the speed of a bullet, accelerating its claw at 10,000 g. The strike creates cavitation bubbles that briefly reach the temperature of the Sun's surface.
About 74,000 years ago a supervolcano in Sumatra erupted with such force it may have reduced the entire human population to as few as 3,000 to 10,000 individuals. We almost did not make it.
Octopuses have nine brains. One central brain plus a smaller brain in each of the eight arms. The arms can react and decide independently of the central brain.

In 1919 a storage tank in Boston exploded and released 2.3 million gallons of molasses through the streets at 35 miles per hour. The wave killed 21 people and injured 150. The neighbourhood smelled of molasses for decades.

In 1971, Soviet engineers were drilling for gas in the Karakum desert. The ground collapsed. A crater opened. Gas started escaping. So they did what seemed logical. They lit it on fire. Thinking it would burn out in a few weeks. It is still burning today. Fifty years later. Thirty metres wide. Deep
The Salar de Uyuni salt flat in Bolivia is so large and so perfectly flat that it becomes a near-perfect mirror when covered by a thin layer of water. It is used to calibrate satellites in orbit.

claim: Three brand-new airliners exploded at altitude for the same reason: their windows were square. Corners crack first. Investigators pulled wreckage from the floor of the Mediterranean and reassembled it piece by piece in a hangar at Farnborough. Each pressurisation cycle had bent the fuselage in and out. After roughly 3,000 flights, the cracks at the window corners joined up. The Comet was grounded and eventually replaced by the Boeing 707. The Americans had been watching closely.

claim:
The United States built a nuclear-powered cruise missile so radioactive that no one could approach it after a test run. Project Pluto, developed from 1957, used an unshielded reactor as its engine. It could fly faster than sound at low altitude for thousands of miles, delivering warheads across an entire continent.

There was nowhere safe to fly it.

The reactor exhaust would irradiate everything beneath its flight path. The launch site had to be abandoned immediately after each test. There was no way to stop it once airborne, and no plan for what happened after the final warhead dropped. The programme was cancelled in 1964, not because the missile failed, but because it worked.
reel_title: The Missile Too Radioactive To Fly

claim: Lord Thomson, Britain's Secretary of State for Air, booked himself onto the R101's maiden voyage to India in 1930 and refused to let anyone postpone it. The R101 was the largest airship ever built. It was also behind schedule, over its safe weight limit, and carrying unfinished repairs. It flew anyway, in a storm. Eight hours after leaving England it struck a hillside in northern France. Forty-eight of the fifty-four people aboard died. Lord Thomson was among them. Britain's entire state airship programme was shut down within the year. The private competitor it had been racing was cancelled too.

claim:
In 1983, five men died on the Byford Dolphin because someone opened a hatch too soon. Four saturation divers were living in a pressurised chamber at nine atmospheres, the equivalent of 90 metres underwater. The hatch connecting their chamber to the diving bell had to be sealed before pressure could shift.

It was not sealed.

The chamber dropped from nine atmospheres to one in a fraction of a second. Four divers died instantly. One was found outside the chamber. The hatch opening was 60 centimetres across. A fifth diver, still in the bell, lost his arm to the pressure wave. The official report runs to hundreds of pages. The cause takes one line.
reel_title: The Hatch Nobody Should Have Opened

claim:
European police spent sixteen years hunting a serial killer who had never been near a crime scene. Her DNA kept appearing at over forty sites across six countries: murders, robberies, the fatal shooting of a police officer in Heilbronn in 2007. She had no name. Interpol were involved.

The DNA was on the swabs.

Every swab used to collect crime scene evidence had come from the same factory in Bavaria. One worker there had been contaminating the packaging. Police had spent sixteen years hunting the fingerprint of a woman who packed laboratory supplies for a living. The enquiry that found this took about two weeks.

claim:
California's largest lake was created entirely by accident and nobody could stop it for twenty-two months. In 1905, a broken irrigation canal let the Colorado River pour freely into the Salton Sink, a desert hollow 70 metres below sea level. Engineers built barrier after barrier. The river broke through every one.

By the time they plugged it, the lake was 56 kilometres long and 19 wide. Nobody planned it. Nobody wanted it. In the 1950s it became a resort, with speedboat races and a yacht club. Then agricultural runoff with nowhere to drain made the water toxic. The Salton Sea is still there. Still shrinking. Still getting saltier.

claim:
In 1943, Britain cancelled a warship project because it worked too slowly, not because it failed. The ship was made of ice. Specifically pykrete: ice mixed with sawdust, stronger than concrete, and almost impossible to melt.

The Allies built a working prototype.

The Royal Navy tested it on a lake in Canada. It floated. It held its shape through the summer. The full design called for a 600-metre platform to counter German U-boats in the mid-Atlantic. By the time construction could begin, the Allies had secured airfields in the Azores. The problem had gone away. The prototype sat on the lake for three summers before it finally melted.

claim:
London's Millennium Bridge started swaying because the people crossing it were trying not to fall over.

It opened in June 2000. On the first day, 90,000 people crossed it.

Each person unconsciously shifted their weight sideways to stay upright. That put lateral force on the bridge. The bridge swayed more. More people fell into the same rhythm to compensate. The force multiplied. Engineers had spent years modelling vertical loads, wind, traffic. Nobody had modelled a crowd of humans automatically synchronising their steps against a wobble. The bridge closed after three days. The retrofit took two years and cost five million pounds. The engineering review described it as an "unexpected resonance phenomenon." The bridge had been open for a weekend.

claim:
Project Stormfury spent eighteen years seeding real Atlantic hurricanes with silver iodide, then discovered the clouds it was treating would have changed on their own anyway. The programme began in 1962. Aircraft flew into active storms and released chemicals designed to break up the eyewall and slow the winds. Several hurricanes appeared to weaken. Funding continued.

The clouds were already going to do that.

It turned out the storms selected for treatment were full of clouds that naturally contract and reform. There was no valid control. Nobody had checked. The programme was cancelled in 1983. Eighteen years of experiments on living storms, and the result was a shrug.
reel_title: They Seeded Hurricanes. For 18 Years. It Did Nothing.

claim: Britain demolished two villages to extend an airfield for an airliner that never carried a paying passenger. The Bristol Brabazon first flew in 1949. It was enormous: ten abreast seating, a cocktail lounge, range enough to cross the Atlantic non-stop. The government had ordered it specifically for transatlantic routes. BOAC, the airline that was supposed to operate it, decided it didn't want it. The aircraft needed runways longer than any airport in America could offer. No carrier ever bought one. All eight aircraft were scrapped. The two villages, Charlton and Newnham, were gone before anyone had found out the plane had no customers.

claim:
Eben Byers drank around 1,400 bottles of radioactive water because his doctor told him it was good for him. The product was called Radithor -- radium dissolved in distilled water, sold across America in the late 1920s as a vitalising tonic.

His jaw fell off.

The bones in his skull were dissolving. Holes opened across his face. By 1931 he weighed under 50 kilograms. The Wall Street Journal ran the story under the headline: "The Radium Water Worked Fine Until His Jaw Fell Off." The FDA moved to regulate radioactive patent medicines the following year. The manufacturer was never prosecuted.

claim:
In 1980, a Texaco oil drill punched through the ceiling of an active salt mine and accidentally drained an entire lake. The drill rig was floating on Lake Peigneur in Louisiana. The Diamond Crystal Salt Company had been mining directly underneath it for years. Neither company had told the other.

The lake disappeared in three hours.

The vortex widened as dissolving salt enlarged the hole. Eleven barges were sucked under. Two oil platforms followed. A parking lot vanished. Part of a botanical garden went with it. The outflow canal reversed direction and pulled nine barges back to the surface. Lake Peigneur refilled through the canal from the Gulf of Mexico. It has been saltwater ever since. Nobody went to prison.
reel_title: One Drill. No Lake.

claim:
A hydrogen bomb landed in a North Carolina field in 1961 and failed to detonate because of a single faulty switch. Five of its six arming steps had completed automatically on the way down.

The switch was not to spec.

The weapon was 260 times more powerful than Hiroshima. It had fallen from a B-52 that broke apart mid-flight over Goldsboro. The other bomb buried itself twelve metres into waterlogged farmland. The warhead was never recovered. It is still down there. The US government bought a small easement over the field and has not said much about it since.
reel_title: The Bomb That Nearly Armed Itself
